lines.text: One molecular formula can describe substances with different properties. Their atom connections reveal why.

Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae. In chain isomerism the carbon skeleton differs. In positional isomerism the same functional group or multiple bond occupies a different position on the same skeleton. In functional group isomerism the functional groups differ. Butane and two methylpropane show chain isomerism, propan one ol and propan two ol show positional isomerism, ethanol and methoxymethane show functional group isomerism.
Compare the displayed or structural formulae before thinking about three dimensional shape.
Same molecular formula, different structural formulae. Types, chain, positional, functional group.
How would you distinguish positional isomerism from functional group isomerism?
Two molecules can have exactly the same atom connections and still be distinct.

Stereoisomers have the same structural formula but different arrangements of atoms in space. The two types here are geometrical, cis or trans, isomerism and optical isomerism. Geometrical forms arise from restricted rotation, optical isomers arise around a chiral centre. E or Z nomenclature is acceptable but not required by this syllabus. When classifying a pair, first compare their connectivity, different connections mean structural isomerism, matching connections permit stereoisomerism.
Both categories share a molecular formula, but stereoisomers share a structural formula too.
Same structural formula, different spatial arrangement. Types, geometrical and optical.
Why is matching molecular formula alone insufficient to establish stereoisomerism?
A double bond locks some arrangements into separate molecules.

In an alkene, the pi bond comes from sideways overlap of p orbitals. Rotation about C equals C would destroy that overlap, so rotation is restricted. Geometrical, cis or trans, isomerism is possible only when each double bond carbon is attached to two different groups. In but two ene, the methyl groups are on the same side in the cis form and opposite sides in the trans form. But one ene fails because its terminal carbon bears two H atoms.
Apply the two different groups test to both C equals C carbons before drawing isomers.
pi bond restricts C equals C rotation. Each C equals C carbon needs two different groups. Cis, same side, trans, opposite sides.
Why does C H two equals C H C H three have no cis or trans pair?
A molecule and its mirror image can have identical bonds yet fail to overlap.

A chiral centre in these organic molecules is a tetrahedral carbon bonded to four different groups. Its two arrangements are optical isomers called enantiomers, non superimposable mirror images. Compare complete groups, not just the atoms directly bonded to carbon. For example, the central carbon of butan two ol has H, O H, C H three and C H two C H three and is chiral, propan two ol has two C H three groups and is not. Molecules can contain more than one chiral centre, symmetry must be considered when counting distinct stereoisomers.
This is the optical branch of stereoisomerism.
Chiral carbon, four different groups. Enantiomers, non superimposable mirror images. More than one chiral centre is possible.
What makes butan two ol chiral but propan two ol achiral?
A complex structure can contain both chiral centres and geometrical alternatives.

For a given structural formula, inspect tetrahedral carbons and compare all four attached groups, include the full paths around a ring when deciding whether two groups match. Mark a carbon as chiral only if all four differ. For an alkene, inspect both C equals C carbons, each must carry two different groups for cis or trans isomerism. In cyclic compounds, restricted rotation of the ring allows substituents on different ring carbons to occupy the same or opposite faces. Thus one, two dichlorocyclobutane can have cis or trans forms, while one, one dichlorocyclobutane cannot.
These checks apply the definitions to displayed, structural and skeletal formulae.
Test four complete groups at a tetrahedral carbon. Test both carbons of each C equals C. In rings compare same and opposite faces.
Why can two paths from a substituted ring carbon be different?
Counting isomers accurately requires a method that catches each structure once.

Start with the known molecular formula and any stated restrictions. List distinct carbon skeletons, then allowed functional groups and positions, checking every structure has the right atom count and valencies. Remove structures that become identical when the chain is numbered from the opposite end or a symmetric molecule is turned around. Next split eligible alkenes or substituted rings into geometrical isomers and check tetrahedral carbons for optical isomers. Independent binary choices can multiply, but symmetry can make two nominal combinations identical. For C four H eight acyclic alkenes, the structural isomers are but one ene, but two ene and two methylpropene, splitting but two ene into cis and trans gives four compounds overall.
Use structural isomerism first, then apply geometrical and optical tests.

thirteen point four Isomerism, structural isomerism and stereoisomerism.
In one breath.
Isomers share a molecular formula. First decide whether their atom connections differ, then test structures with the same connections for distinct arrangements in space.
Key ideas.

Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae. In chain isomerism, the carbon skeleton differs, butane and two methylpropane are examples. In positional isomerism, the same functional group or multiple bond moves to another position on the same skeleton, as in propan one ol and propan two ol. In functional group isomerism, the functional groups differ, as in ethanol and methoxymethane, both C two H six O. Be precise, a shared molecular formula alone does not tell you which type of isomerism is present.

Stereoisomers have the same structural formula but different arrangements of atoms in space. The syllabus divides these into geometrical, cis or trans, isomerism and optical isomerism. E or Z names are acceptable but are not required here.

For an alkene, sideways p orbital overlap creates a pi bond. Rotating about C double bond C would break this overlap, so rotation is restricted. A cis or trans pair exists only when each double bond carbon has two different attached groups. In but two ene, the two methyl groups are on the same side in the cis form and opposite sides in the trans form. But one ene has a terminal C H two double bond carbon with two identical hydrogen atoms, so it has no cis or trans pair. The same two group test applies to each double bond in a molecule with several alkenes.

A chiral centre in these compounds is a tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups. Its two optical isomers, or enantiomers, are non superimposable mirror images. Carbon two of butan two ol is attached to H, O H, C H three and C H two C H three, so it is chiral. Carbon two of propan two ol has two methyl groups and is not. A compound can have more than one chiral centre.
Method.

From a molecular formula, list distinct carbon skeletons, possible functional groups and positions. Check each formula's atom count and carbon valencies. Reverse the numbering or turn a symmetric skeleton around to remove duplicates.

For every C double bond C bond, compare both substituents on each double bond carbon. Where both carbons pass, add cis or trans arrangements. In a cyclic compound, substituents on different ring carbons may be on the same or opposite face of the ring.

Inspect tetrahedral carbons for four different complete groups. In rings, trace both paths around the ring before deciding whether they are identical. Add optical isomers where appropriate, then compare complete structures for symmetry duplicates.
Worked example.

Deduce all acyclic alkene isomers of C four H eight, including stereoisomers. List the three structural isomers, but one ene, but two ene and two methylpropene. But one ene and two methylpropene each have two identical groups at one alkene carbon. But two ene has two different groups on each alkene carbon, so it gives cis but two ene and trans but two ene. The distinct compounds are therefore but one ene, cis but two ene, trans but two ene and two methylpropene, four.
Traps.
Trap, Calling any two compounds with the same molecular formula stereoisomers. Why it's wrong, Their atom connections may differ. Instead, Compare structural formulae first.
Trap, Counting every double bond as two geometrical forms. Why it's wrong, A double bond carbon may have two identical groups. Instead, Test both carbons of each C double bond C.
Trap, Assuming four bonds make a carbon chiral. Why it's wrong, Two attached groups may be identical, even if their ring paths need tracing. Instead, Compare all four complete groups.

Trap, Adding independent stereochemical choices or counting mirror equivalent cases twice. Why it's wrong, Independent choices multiply, and symmetry can collapse apparent combinations. Instead, Enumerate the actual distinct structures.
Exam technique.

For describe or define, include both what remains the same and what differs. For identify, mark the relevant carbon or bond and state the groups that prove the test. For deduce and determine, show a systematic list before giving a total. If a question says structural isomerism only, do not count cis or trans or optical pairs separately, if it asks for all isomers, check both structural and stereochemical alternatives.
